## Quiz 1 Review

#### High Level

• Need to solve large problems n with constant-sized code, correctly and efficiently 
• Analyzing running time: How to count? – Asymptotics – Recurrences (substitution, tree method, Master Theorem) – Model of computation: Word-RAM, Comparison 
• How to solve an algorithms problem – Reduce to a problem you know how to solve ∗ Use an algorithm you know (e.g. sort) ∗ Use a data structure you know (e.g. search) – Design a new recursive algorithm (harder, mostly in 6.046) ∗ Brute Force ∗ Decrease & Conquer ∗ Divide & Conquer (like merge sort) ∗ Dynamic Programming (later in 6.006!) ∗ Greedy/Incremental

Questions to ask:

• Is this a Mechanical, Reduction, or Modification type problem? 
• Is this problem about data structures? sorting? both?

• If stuck, is there an easy way to get a correct but inefficient algorithm? Question yourself if you are: 
• Trying to compute decimals, rationals, or real numbers

Problem 1. Restaurant Lineup (S19 Q1) 
Popular restaurant Criminal Seafood does not take reservations, but maintains a wait list where 
customers who have been on the wait list longer are seated earlier. Sometimes customers decide to 
eat somewhere else, so the restaurant must remove them from the wait list. Assume each customer 
has a different name, and no two customers are added to the wait list at the exact same time. Design 
a database to help Criminal Seafood maintain its wait list supporting the following operations, each 
in O(1) time. State whether each operation running time is worst-case, amortized, and/or expected. 
build() initialize an empty database 
add name(x) add name x to the back of the wait list 
remove name(x) remove name x from the wait list 
seat() remove and return the name of the customer from the front of the wait list 
Solution: Maintain a doubly-linked list containing customers on the wait list in order, maintaining 
a pointer to the front of the linked list corresponding to the front of the wait list, and a pointer to 
the back of the linked list corresponding to the back of the wait list. Also maintain a hash table 
mapping each customer name to the linked list node containing that customer. To implement 
add name(x), create a new linked list node containing name x and add it to the back of the 
linked list in worst-case O(1) time. Then add name x to the hash table pointing to the newly 
created node in amortized expected O(1) time. To implement remove name(x), lookup name 
x in the hash table in and remove the mapped node from the linked list in expected O(1) time. 
Lastly, to implement seat(), remove the node from the front of the linked list containing name 
x, remove name x from the hash table, and then return x, in amortized expected O(1) time. 

Problem 2. Rainy Research (S19 Q1) 
Mether Wan is a scientist who studies global rainfall. Mether often receives data measurements 
from a large set of deployed sensors. Each collected data measurement is a triple of integers 
(r, `,t), where r is a positive amount of rainfall measured at latitude ` at time t. The peak rainfall 
at latitude ` since time t is the maximum rainfall of any measurement at latitude ` measured at a 
time greater than or equal to t (or zero if no such measurement exists). Describe a database that 
can store Mether’s sensor data and support the following operations, each in worst-case O(log n) 
time where n is the number of measurements in the database at the time of the operation. 
build() initialize an empty database 

record data(r, `,t) add a rainfall measurement r at latitude ` at time t peak rainfall(`,t) return the peak rainfall at latitude ` since time t

Solution: Maintain a Set AVL tree L storing distinct measurement latitudes, where each latitude ` maps to a rainfall Set AVL tree R(`) containing all measurement triples with latitude `, keyed by time. We only store nodes associated with measurements, so the height of each Set AVL tree is bounded by O(log n). For each rainfall tree, augment each node p with the maximum rainfall p.m of any measurement within p’s subtree. This augmentation can be maintained in constant time at a node p by taking the maximum of the rainfall at p and the augmented maximums of p’s left and right children (if they exist); thus this augmentation can be maintained without effecting the asymptotic running time of standard AVL tree operations.

To implement record data(r, `,t), search L for latitude ` in worst-case O(log n) time. If ` does not exist in L, insert a new node corresponding to ` mapping to a new empty rainfall Set AVL tree, also in O(log n) time. In either case, insert the measurement triple to R(`), for a total running time of worst-case O(log n). To implement peak rainfall(`,t), search L for latitude ` in worst-case O(log n) time. If ` does not exist, return zero. Otherwise, perform a one-sided range query on R(`) to find the peak rainfall at latitude ` since time t. Specifically, let peak(v,t) be the maximum rainfall of any measurement in node v’s subtree measured at time ≥ t (or zero if v is not a node):

( max { v.item.r, v.right.m, peak(v.lef t,t)} if v.t ≥ t peak(v,t) = . peak(v.right,t) if v.t < t Then peak rainfall is simply peak(v,t) with v being the root of the tree, which can be computed using at most O(log n) recursive calls. So this operation runs in worst-case O(log n) time. Note, this problem can also be solved where each latitude AVL tree is keyed by rainfall, augment ing nodes with maximum time in subtree. We leave this as an exercise to the reader.

Here is the ruthlessly condensed, exam-maximizing summary, sourced entirely from MIT OCW (6.006 Spring 2020) official materials.

---

## 1. Exact List of Topics (Lectures 1–8)

*Source: MIT 6.006 Spring 2020 Calendar (ocw.mit.edu) — Lectures 1-8 are the only content tested.*

| Lecture | Topic | Core Concepts |
|---|---|---|
| L1 | Intro + Algorithm Analysis | Asymptotics (O, Ω, Θ), Word-RAM model, problem reduction |
| L2 | Data Structures + Dynamic Arrays | Static array, linked list, dynamic array (amortized O(1) append) |
| L3 | Sorting | Insertion sort, selection sort, merge sort, comparison model Ω(n log n) lower bound |
| L4 | Hashing | Direct-access array, hash table (chaining), universal hashing, expected O(1) ops |
| L5 | Linear Sorting | Counting sort (O(n+u)), radix sort (O(n log_u c)) — when keys are integers with bounded range |
| L6 | Binary Trees, Part 1 | Set/Sequence interface, BST property, traversal order, tree navigation |
| L7 | Binary Trees, Part 2: AVL | AVL trees, rotations (left/right), height-balance property, height ≤ 2 log₂(n+1) |
| L8 | Binary Heaps | Min/max-heap property, implicit array representation, build/insert/extract, heap sort |

**Meta-point:** Quiz 1 content is L1–L8 **only**. L9 (BFS) is NOT on Quiz 1, despite appearing in some reviews for context.

---

## 2. Jason Ku's Problem-Solving Framework (from the Review)

*Source: Quiz 1 Review Solutions PDF (MIT6_006S20_review1_sol.pdf) — directly from Jason Ku's review session.*

**The pyramid of approach, in priority order:**

### Step 1: Reduce to a known algorithm or data structure
> "How to solve an algorithms problem — Reduce to a problem you know how to solve. Use an algorithm you know (e.g. sort). Use a data structure you know (e.g. search)."

- **Sorting problems** → pick the right sort from the table below
- **Data structure problems** → choose Sequence ops or Set ops, then pick the DS

### Step 2: Problem type triage (ask yourself in order)
1. **Is this Mechanical, Reduction, or Modification?**
   - *Mechanical* = tests whether you know how core material works (e.g. "trace heap delete-max")
   - *Reduction* = tests whether you can apply core material to new scenario (≈70% of exam)
   - *Modification* = tests whether you can adapt core material (augmentation, amortization)
2. **Is this about data structures? sorting? both?**
3. **If data structures: Sequence ops or Set ops or both?**
4. **If stuck: can I get a correct but inefficient algorithm quickly?** (partial credit!)

### Step 3: For data structure design problems
- First solve conceptually using Sorting or Set/Sequence interfaces
- *Then* choose concrete algorithm/data structure
- **Always:** describe data structures used, what data they store, and their invariants
- **Always:** implement every operation asked for
- **Always:** separate and label parts of your solution

---

## 3. The Decision Tables (from the Review Solutions PDF)

These are the exact tables Jason Ku put in the review. **Memorize them for your cheat sheet.**

### Sorting Algorithm Decision Table

```
Algorithm         Time O(·)    In-place?  Stable?   When to pick
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Insertion Sort    O(n + d)      Y          Y         n small OR d-proximate (d inversions)
Selection Sort    O(n²)         Y          N         O(n) swaps, simple
Merge Sort        O(n log n)    N          Y         Stable, optimal comparison; general-purpose
AVL Sort          O(n log n)    N          Y         Need dynamic inserts/deletes mid-sort
Heap Sort         O(n log n)    Y          N         Low space, optimal comparison; in-place
Counting Sort     O(n + u)      N          Y         Keys are integers with range u = O(n)
Radix Sort        O(n log_u c)  N          Y         Keys are integers with O(n^c) range,
                                                     break into base-b digits
```

**Decision tree for sorting:**
1. **Can you compare?** If comparison is the only operation → Ω(n log n) lower bound → merge sort or heap sort.
2. **Are keys bounded integers?** If range u = O(n) → counting sort O(n). If range u = O(n^c) → radix sort O(n).
3. **Need in-place?** Heap sort (Y) or insertion sort (Y). Merge sort is N.
4. **Need stable?** Merge sort, counting sort, radix sort, insertion sort are Y. Selection sort, heap sort are N.
5. **Already nearly sorted (k-proximate)?** Insertion sort O(nk).
6. **Need to interleave sorts with dynamic updates?** AVL Sort.

### Data Structure Decision Table — Sequence Operations

```
DS              get_at/set_at  insert_first/delete_first  insert_last/delete_last  insert_at/delete_at
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Array           O(1)           O(n)                       O(n)                     O(n)
Linked List     O(n)           O(1)                       O(1) (w/ tail ptr)      O(n)
Dynamic Array   O(1)           O(n)                       O(1) amortized           O(n)
Sequence AVL    O(log n)       O(log n)                   O(log n)                 O(log n)
```

**Pick Sequence AVL when:** You need all operations in O(log n) — the balanced, do-everything tree.

### Data Structure Decision Table — Set Operations

```
DS              build  find(k)  insert  delete  min/max  prev/next
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Array           n      n        n       n       n        n
Sorted Array    n log n log n   n       n       1        log n
Direct Access   u      1        1       u       u        u
Hash Table      n(e)   1(e)     1(a)(e) n       n        n
Set AVL         n log n log n   log n   log n   log n    log n
```

**Pick Hash Table when:** You need fast find/insert/delete by key and **don't** need order ops (min/max/prev/next).

**Pick Set AVL when:** You need fast find/insert/delete **AND** need order ops (min/max/prev/next).

### Priority Queue Operations

```
DS              build  insert  delete_max  find_max
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Dynamic Array   1(a)   1(a)    n           n
Sorted Dyn Arr  n log n n      1(a)        1
Set AVL         n log n log n  log n       log n
Binary Heap     n(a)   log n   log n       n(a)  ← build can be O(n)
```

**Pick Binary Heap when:** You need a priority queue. Build in O(n), insert/extract in O(log n). Most efficient PQ.

---

## 4. Most Common Exam Problem Patterns (from the Actual Quiz)

*Source: MIT6_006S20_q1.pdf and solutions — the actual Spring 2020 Quiz 1.*

| Problem Type | What They Test | Point Value | How to Solve |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical: Running-time analysis** (Q2 Frequentest) | Hash table (expected vs worst-case) vs direct-access array | 8 pts | Know: hash table insert/lookup is O(1) expected but O(n) worst-case. Direct-access is O(n+u). Don't say "amortized" for hash tables. |
| **Mechanical: Heap properties** (Q3 Haphazard Heap) | Min-heap ordering: smallest must be root, 3rd smallest in first 3 levels, largest in any leaf | 10 pts | Draw the tree shape. Smallest = index 0. 3rd smallest = any of indices 1–6 (levels 1-2). Largest = any leaf (indices 4–9). |
| **Mechanical: Heap delete-max / AVL delete** (Q4 Transforming Trees) | Heap array representation + delete-max procedure; AVL Sequence Tree traversal-order delete + rotations | 10 pts | Heap: swap root with last leaf, pop, bubble down. AVL Sequence: delete by traversal order index, then rebalance with rotations. |
| **Reduction: Pick the right sort** (Q5 Sorting Sock) | Map scenario constraints → sorting algorithm choice | 20 pts | Four subproblems. Key: bounded integer → counting/radix; comparison only → merge sort; max-finding only → selection sort (O(n)); exponential range → radix. |
| **Reduction: Search with hash table** (Q6 Triple Sum) | Reduce 3SUM to 2SUM via hash table | 15 pts | Store all O(n²) pair-sums in hash table, then check each c. Expected O(n²). |
| **Modification: Augmented AVL** (Q7 Where Am I) | Walk up AVL tree using subtree sizes to compute inorder index | 15 pts | Starting from node v: count nodes before v in left subtree; walk up: if right child, add 1 + parent.left.size. O(log n). |
| **Design: Data structure design** (Q8 Methane Menace, Q9 Vapor Invite) | Combine multiple data structures for novel scenario | 40 pts total (20 ea) | Typically: hash table + heap OR multiple AVL trees with augmentation. State invariants. Implement each operation separately. |

---

## 5. Top 5 Mistakes Students Make (from the Official Solutions)

*Source: "Common Mistakes:" annotations in the Quiz 1 Solutions PDF (MIT6_006S20_q1_sol.pdf). These are the exact errors the graders flagged.*

### 1. Confusing "amortized" with "expected"
> **Common Mistakes:** "Saying doing a O(1)-time operation m times takes amortized O(m) time."

Hash table ops are **expected** O(1), not amortized. Dynamic array append is **amortized** O(1), not expected. These are different guarantees — know which is which.

### 2. Heap: thinking 3rd smallest must be at index 1 or 2
> **Common Mistakes:** "Incorrectly assuming third smallest must be in either B or C."

In a 10-element min-heap, the 3rd smallest can be **anywhere in the first 3 levels** (indices 1 through 6), not just the two children of the root. Many students restrict it too much.

### 3. Heap: thinking the largest must be in the bottom row
> **Common Mistakes:** "Thinking the largest integer must be in the bottom level (instead of in any leaf)."

The largest element in a min-heap is any leaf. For a 10-element heap, leaves are indices 4–9 (not just the bottom row of the implicit tree).

### 4. Heap: confusing heap order with traversal order / AVL: using 1-indexing
> **Common Mistakes:** "Not building heap correctly (e.g., confusing heap order with traversal order)" and "Indexing by heap order instead of traversal order (or using 1-indexing)."

Sequence AVL uses **zero-indexed** traversal order (inorder). Heap array is level-order. Do not mix them. A Sequence AVL delete_at(3) removes the 4th item in traversal order, not the 4th array slot.

### 5. AVL: deleting without rebalancing / Radix overuse
> **Common Mistakes:** "Deleting the item but not rebalancing the tree to satisfy the AVL Property."

After any AVL modification, you must walk back up applying rotations. Also: **"Using Radix sort for every answer"** (Jason Ku's warning) — if keys aren't bounded integers, radix doesn't apply.

**Honorable mention:** Claiming Ω(n log n) when the data admits a linear sort (or vice versa). Always ask: *are the keys integers with a bounded range?* If yes, you can beat n log n.

---

## Final Cheat-Sheet Notes (for your one double-sided letter sheet)

1. **Hash table:** expected O(1) find/insert; worst-case O(n). Not amortized.
2. **Dynamic array:** amortized O(1) insert_last; worst-case O(n).
3. **Binary heap:** smallest in min-heap = root; largest = any leaf. Delete-min: swap with last leaf, bubble down.
4. **AVL tree height:** ≤ 2 log₂(n+1). All ops O(log n). Rotations: left, right, left-right, right-left.
5. **Sequence vs Set:** Sequence = order you impose (traversal order, indices). Set = order intrinsic to keys.
6. **When stuck:** a correct O(n²) solution gets significant partial credit. Write *something* correct.
7. **Master Theorem:** For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a). Three cases.
8. **Comparison sort lower bound:** Ω(n log n). If only comparisons allowed, you can't beat merge sort.
